primary_topics: Address at the CIDA Asia Field Representatives Meeting, May 8, 2008 -- CIDA arranged the 2002 Ottawa visit and the JURIS MOU signing

The Ottawa encounter with Canadian justices (June 18, 2002): Justice L'Heureux-Dubé's observation that Philippine decisions cite American but never Canadian SC; CJP's response; the pledge fulfilled in People v. Genosa (battered woman syndrome, first Canadian citation in Philippine jurisprudence)

CJP's vision-mission statement as CJ: four Ins (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence); plague of ships (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship); four ACID problems (access, corruption, incompetence, delay); twin goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity
Pierre Elliott Trudeau's 'just society' as the Canadian analog to CJP's liberty-and-prosperity philosophy; McLachlin's Ateneo honorary doctorate definition of the just society
sub_topics: CIDA-JURIS context: CIDA arranged the Ottawa visit and the signing of the JURIS MOU; the Ottawa encounter with Canadian justices was part of that institutional relationship

Ottawa encounter: Chief Justice McLachlin hosted lunch in the Judges' Dining Room, June 18, 2002; Philippine delegation: CJ Davide, Justice Herrera and CJP; Senior Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dubé noted that Philippine decisions liberally cite US SC (Holmes, Black, Frankfurter) but not Canadian; 'For a moment, our delegation was stunned to speechlessness'; CJP replied: 'I must admit that Your Honor is correct... I, too, have yet to read a Canadian decision citing the Philippine Supreme Court.' -- 'the exchange of banter broke the proverbial ice'

The pledge fulfilled: CJP 'took the banter to heart'; upon returning, penned People v. Genosa, 'adopting for the first time the battered woman syndrome as a form of self-defense, or at least a mitigating circumstance, in a prosecution for parricide'; expressly cited a Canadian SC decision as authority -- 'that encounter may have been a minor incident in the great history of the Canadian Court, but it was a major event of my judicial career'

Vision-mission as CJ: four Ins (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence); resist influence, interference, indifference and insolence; 'impervious to the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship'; continue the APJR with special focus on four ACID problems (access, corruption, incompetence, delay)
Twin goals: safeguarding liberty (traditional forte; strict scrutiny) and nurturing prosperity (deferential interpretation for economic matters)

Trudeau's just society: captured by Pierre Elliott Trudeau in his advocacy of 'the just society'; per McLachlin upon receiving her Ateneo honorary doctorate: 'a society governed by the rule of law and built on the values of democracy, equality and liberty. It means a society in which all can participate, where all can pursue a dream, where all enjoy basic liberties of expression, association and movement.'

CIDA's global contribution: 'the peoples of the Philippines and the world are aflame with gratitude and praise for Canada because Canadians want to share the blessings of their just society with the rest of mankind through CIDA'

stances.claim: People v. Genosa is the most consequential outcome of a social interaction in CJP's judicial career: a casual banter with Justice L'Heureux-Dubé about citation practices led CJP to become the first Philippine justice to cite a Canadian SC decision as authority -- in a landmark case on battered woman syndrome. The Ottawa encounter that seemed minor was actually transformative.

stances.claim: The plague-of-ships metaphor (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship) is CJP's most memorable formulation of the sources of judicial independence failure. The four -ship words describe four corrupting relational influences that pull judges toward favoritism and away from the rule of law.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered May 8, 2008 at the CIDA Asia Field Representatives Meeting -- CIDA having arranged the 2002 Ottawa visit and the JURIS (Judicial Reform Initiative Support Project) MOU signing -- this address by CJP centers on the most memorable episode of his judicial career: the June 18, 2002 lunch at the Supreme Court of Canada, hosted by CJ Beverley McLachlin in the Judges' Dining Room. The Philippine delegation (CJ Davide, Justice Herrera and CJP) was challenged by Senior Justice Claire L'Heureux-Dubé, who noted that Philippine decisions liberally cite Holmes, Black and Frankfurter 'but I have yet to see one that cites our Canadian justices.' CJP replied honestly: 'I, too, have yet to read a Canadian decision citing the Philippine Supreme Court.' He 'took the banter to heart': upon returning, he penned People v. Genosa -- 'adopting for the first time the battered woman syndrome as a form of self-defense, or at least a mitigating circumstance, in a prosecution for parricide' -- and expressly cited a Canadian SC decision as authority. 'That encounter may have been a minor incident in the great history of the Canadian Court, but it was a major event of my judicial career.' He presents his vision-mission as CJ: four Ins (independence, integrity, industry, intelligence); impervious to the 'plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship'; four ACID problems (access, corruption, incompetence, delay); twin goals of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law. He closes with Pierre Elliott Trudeau's 'just society' as the Canadian analog -- defined by McLachlin at her Ateneo honorary doctorate speech as 'a society governed by the rule of law and built on the values of democracy, equality and liberty... where all can participate, where all can pursue a dream, where all enjoy basic liberties of expression, association and movement' -- and thanks CIDA for sharing this vision with the Philippines.
